name: Alan Rickman
milestone_by_age_26: Applied to RADA at age 26 (1972) after working as a graphic designer; no material acting milestone by 26 — his professional acting career began after RADA training, with RSC joining at 32 and film fame arriving with Die Hard (1988) at age 42.

name: Richard Stallman
milestone_by_age_26: Developed Emacs, the first extensible customizable self-documenting display editor, at the MIT AI Lab in 1976 (age 23), and published the EMACS paper as MIT AI Memo 519 in June 1979 (age 26).
early_history_summary: Stallman was programming from high school, hired at the IBM New York Scientific Center in summer 1970, and became a programmer at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in 1971 during his first year at Harvard. He quickly became a central figure in the MIT hacker community, developing system software including Emacs (1976) and the AI technique of dependency-directed backtracking (1975), all before age 26.
family_context_summary: Born in Manhattan in 1953 to a family of Jewish heritage. He had a troublesome relationship with his parents and did not feel he had a proper home, finding a sense of belonging only at Harvard and the MIT AI Lab.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of parental computing or technical expertise.
primary_early_advantage_tags: MIT AI Lab, Harvard, PDP-10, ITS, hacker community, time-sharing systems
evidence_summary: Stallman gained access to the MIT AI Lab — the premier computing research environment of the era — during his first year at Harvard in 1971, and became a central figure in its hacker community. He had rare early access to PDP-10 computers and the ITS time-sharing system, which were extremely scarce for the era. His sustained immersion in this elite ecosystem enabled him to develop Emacs by age 23. Family background provided no domain advantage; his drive was self-created, partly catalyzed by feeling like an outsider in his family life. The MIT AI Lab community served as both peer network and mentorship environment.

name: John Walker
milestone_by_age_26: Ran his first sub-four-minute mile in July 1973 (age 21), broke the world mile record with 3:49.4 in August 1975 (age 23) becoming the first man under 3:50, and won Olympic 1500m gold at the 1976 Montreal Games (age 24).
early_history_summary: Walker grew up in Manurewa, New Zealand, running from childhood and excelling in cross country at school. He chose running over tennis at 17 and linked up with coach Arch Jelley, who applied the Arthur Lydiard training system. He made a breakthrough at 19 by defeating Dick Quax, won his first NZ senior title, and ran his first sub-4 mile at 21 before breaking the world record at 23.
family_context_summary: Raised one of three children in Manurewa, New Zealand. His father had him run the mile to and from the shops to pick up the newspaper. No evidence of family financial resources or athletic domain expertise.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of parental athletic or coaching expertise.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Arch Jelley coaching, Arthur Lydiard system, New Zealand running tradition, natural endurance
evidence_summary: Walker benefited from New Zealand's rich middle-distance running tradition and the Arthur Lydiard training methodology, transmitted through his long-term coach Arch Jelley who guided him for 21 years from age 17. His natural running talent was evident from childhood, and he developed through the local club and school system. No evidence of family financial support or parental athletic background; his advantage came from the coaching pipeline and his own physical talent and intense training (80 miles per week). The sustained mentorship of Jelley was the single most important external advantage.

name: Venkatraman Ramakrishnan
milestone_by_age_26: Completed PhD in physics at Ohio University in 1976 (age 24) and began a postdoc at UC San Diego, but no material independently verifiable public milestone by age 26 — his Nobel Prize-winning ribosome structure work came decades later (2000s).

name: Elena Ferrante
milestone_by_age_26: Published her first novel (Troubling Love) in 1992 at approximately age 49; no material literary milestone by age 26 — she is pseudonymous and biographical details are deliberately withheld, with no verifiable early publication or recognition.

name: Novak Djokovic
milestone_by_age_26: Won his first ATP singles title at Amersfoort in July 2006 (age 19), claimed his first Grand Slam title at the 2008 Australian Open (age 20), and by age 26 (2013) had won 6 Grand Slam titles and reached world No. 1.
early_history_summary: Djokovic started playing tennis at age 4 in Kopaonik, Serbia, where his parents ran a pizzeria near three tennis courts. He was identified as a special talent by coach Jelena Gencic at age 6, who trained him for six years. At 13 he moved to Nikola Pilic's academy in Munich. He won the U14 European Championship, claimed his first Futures title at 16, first Challenger title at 17, and broke into the top 100 at 18 before winning his first ATP title at 19.
family_context_summary: Born to Srdjan and Dijana Djokovic in Belgrade. Parents were professional skiers who ran a pizzeria and sports equipment shop in Kopaonik. Family was on a very low budget and took high-interest loans to fund Novak's tennis training. Father made everything subordinate to Novak's development. Two younger brothers also played professional tennis.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were professional skiers and ski instructors, not tennis players. No direct tennis domain expertise was transferred, though the family operated sports-adjacent businesses and recognized athletic talent.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Jelena Gencic mentorship, Pilic academy, early talent recognition, wartime adversity, family sacrifice
evidence_summary: Djokovic's early career was driven by intense early specialization (tennis from age 4), sustained high-quality mentorship from Jelena Gencic (6 years) and Nikola Pilic, and recognition as a prodigy at age 6. His family made enormous financial sacrifices, taking high-interest loans to fund training. The Yugoslav Wars created severe adversity — embargoes prevented international junior travel, NATO bombings disrupted training, and he practiced in a converted swimming pool. This wartime constraint catalyzed urgency and resilience. His parents' ski background provided no tennis domain expertise, but their athletic orientation and total commitment to Novak's development was a critical enabler.

name: Pierre Agostini
milestone_by_age_26: Was still completing his doctoral thesis on UV multilayer dielectric filters at Aix-Marseille University by age 26 (1967); his PhD was awarded in 1968 (age 27) and his Nobel Prize-winning attosecond pulse work came decades later (2000s).

name: Pina Bausch
milestone_by_age_26: Became a soloist at the newly founded Folkwang Dance Studio in Essen in 1962 (age 22) under Kurt Jooss, after winning the Folkwang Leistungspreis (1958), training at Juilliard on a DAAD scholarship (1959-61), and dancing at the Metropolitan Opera and New American Ballet in New York.
early_history_summary: Bausch grew up performing for guests in her parents' restaurant in Solingen, Germany, and joined children's ballet at an early age. At 14 she was accepted into Kurt Jooss's Folkwang School in Essen, a pioneering institution of German expressive dance (Ausdruckstanz), graduating in 1959. She won the Folkwang Leistungspreis in 1958, then studied at Juilliard on a DAAD scholarship, dancing with the New American Ballet and at the Metropolitan Opera before returning to Essen as a soloist in 1962.
family_context_summary: Born into a family that owned a restaurant with guest rooms in Solingen, Germany. Her parents recognized her performing talent when she danced for restaurant guests as a young child. The restaurant environment later influenced her choreography, notably Café Müller.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were restaurateurs, not dancers. No direct dance domain expertise was transferred, but the family restaurant provided an early performance venue and audience exposure.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Kurt Jooss mentorship, Folkwang School, Juilliard, DAAD scholarship, Antony Tudor, early performance exposure
evidence_summary: Bausch's early path was shaped by sustained mentorship from Kurt Jooss at the Folkwang School (ages 14-19), a pioneering institution of German expressive dance that combined ballet with Ausdruckstanz. She then trained at Juilliard under Antony Tudor and others, and danced at the Metropolitan Opera in New York, before returning as a soloist at the Folkwang Dance Studio at 22. The multi-arts environment of the Folkwang School was a distinctive advantage. Her parents' restaurant provided early performance exposure but no direct dance domain expertise. Growing up during WWII in Germany created formative adversity that later informed her choreographic vision.

name: Serge Haroche
milestone_by_age_26: Was a CNRS research associate at ENS working on his doctoral thesis under Claude Cohen-Tannoudji by age 26 (1970); his thesis was defended in 1971 (age 27) and his Nobel Prize-winning quantum optics work came in later decades — no material independently verifiable milestone by 26.

name: Mikhail Leonidovich Gromov
milestone_by_age_26: Completed his doctorate at Leningrad State University in 1969 (age 25) under Vladimir Rokhlin, having published multiple significant papers in geometry and topology from 1967-1969; by approximately 1970 his work 'astounded the world of differential geometry' and he was invited to speak at the International Congress of Mathematicians.
early_history_summary: Gromov entered Leningrad University in 1960 at age 17 and showed exceptional mathematical talent early. He completed his master's degree (equivalent to a PhD in the US) in 1965 at age 22, became an assistant professor in 1967, and earned his doctorate in 1969. His papers from the late 1960s on geometric hypotheses, foliations, and topology were groundbreaking enough that by around 1970 the international differential geometry community was astounded, and he was invited to address the ICM in Nice (though Soviet authorities prevented his attendance).
family_context_summary: Born in Boksitogorsk, Russia. Both parents were pathologists. His mother was the cousin of World Chess Champion Mikhail Botvinnik and mathematician Isaak Moiseevich Rabinovich. His mother gave him 'The Enjoyment of Mathematics' by Rademacher and Toeplitz at age 9, which had a great influence on him.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were medical pathologists, not mathematicians. However, the family had intellectual connections to mathematics and chess through his mother's cousins — World Chess Champion Mikhail Botvinnik and mathematician Isaak Moiseevich Rabinovich — suggesting an intellectually oriented family environment.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Vladimir Rokhlin advisor, Leningrad University, intellectual family, early math exposure, Soviet mathematical tradition
evidence_summary: Gromov's early mathematical development was shaped by his training at Leningrad State University under Vladimir Rokhlin, a significant mathematician who was himself a student of Kolmogorov and Pontryagin. His family had intellectual connections — his mother was cousin to chess champion Botvinnik and mathematician Rabinovich — and she gave him a mathematics book at age 9 that sparked his curiosity. The Soviet mathematical pipeline at Leningrad University was elite, and Gromov's talent was recognized early. His groundbreaking results by age 25-26 were achieved through deep individual work in a resource-constrained Soviet environment, with collaboration from Rokhlin and Eliashberg. Soviet restrictions on travel and communication created adversity but also forced intense local concentration.

name: Robert De Niro
milestone_by_age_26: Appeared in minor independent films (The Wedding Party released 1969, Greetings 1968) by age 26, but had no material acting milestone — his breakout came with Mean Streets (1973, age 30) and his first Oscar for The Godfather Part II (1974, age 31).

name: Antonio Inoki
milestone_by_age_26: Made his professional wrestling debut on September 30, 1960 (age 17) for the Japan Pro Wrestling Alliance under Rikidozan, and by 1963 (age 20) had become one of the most popular stars in Japanese professional wrestling under the ring name Antonio Inoki.
early_history_summary: Born in Yokohama, Inoki's family emigrated to Brazil when he was 14 after his father's death and the collapse of the family coal business. He worked on a coffee plantation and excelled in track and field, winning Brazilian national championships in shot put and discus at 17. Wrestling legend Rikidozan discovered him in Brazil and brought him to Japan, where he debuted professionally at 17. By 1963, he was one of the top young stars in Japanese wrestling alongside Shohei Baba.
family_context_summary: Born into an affluent family in Yokohama with 11 siblings. Father Sajiro Inoki was a businessman and politician who died when Kanji was 5. The family's coal wholesaling business went bankrupt amid the shift from coal to oil, and the family emigrated to Brazil in 1957, where they worked in the coffee industry in poverty.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a businessman and politician. No wrestling or athletic domain expertise in the family. The family's coal business was lost to bankruptcy, providing no inherited business platform.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Rikidozan mentorship, JWA pipeline, postwar wrestling boom, poverty, emigration, physical labor, natural athleticism
evidence_summary: Inoki's path was shaped by severe adversity — his father died when he was 5, the family business went bankrupt, and he emigrated to Brazil at 14 where he did manual labor on a coffee plantation. This physical labor built remarkable conditioning. His natural athletic talent (Brazilian shot put and discus champion at 17) caught the attention of Rikidozan, the father of Japanese pro wrestling, who personally recruited and trained him. The postwar Japanese wrestling boom on television provided a structural wave. Inoki debuted at 17 and became a major star by 20, riding the JWA pipeline and Rikidozan's mentorship. No family financial or domain advantage; his success was self-created through physical talent and the opportunity provided by Rikidozan's discovery.
